title: Methods
text:
This study examines the scale, composition, and evolution of World Bank Group development finance in Costa Rica from 1980 through 2025. The primary analysis is descriptive, centered on IBRD sovereign lending. IFC investments and MIGA guarantees provide separate perspectives on private-sector finance and political risk coverage.
The analysis identifies changes in financing patterns and places them alongside national development indicators. It does not estimate the causal effects of World Bank financing on Costa Rica’s economic or social outcomes.

title: Methods
text:
Project Reconciliation
The World Bank Projects & Operations catalogue provides the project universe and canonical project approval dates. IBRD loan records are matched to projects by project ID. API V2 records supplement project metadata, sector allocations, and abstracts; they are not treated as a complete project inventory.
API V3 records were used to corroborate missing approval dates in V2. Where dates could not be recovered, they remain missing rather than being inferred.
Loan-level financial records are aggregated by project ID before joining project metadata. This prevents multiple loans associated with one project from duplicating project-level records or financial totals.

title: Methods
text:
IBRD Financial Analysis
The analysis filters the IBRD Statement to Costa Rica loan records and excludes guarantees. Original principal and cancellations are retained separately.
Net principal is calculated as:
\[
\text{Net principal} =
\max(\text{Original principal} - \text{Cancellations}, 0)
\]
The zero floor prevents terminated records with no original principal from producing negative net commitments. Projects with fully cancelled loans remain in project counts but contribute no net principal. The undisbursed COVID-19 Vaccines project (P178320) is retained in project counts with zero original principal.
Annual commitments are assigned to the Board Approval Year recorded in the loan statement. Years without approvals are retained as zero in the annual series.

title: Methods
text:
Inflation Adjustment
Nominal IBRD commitments are converted to approximate 2025 dollars using the U.S. GDP deflator:
\[
\text{Real amount}_{2025} =
\text{Nominal amount}_{t}
\times
\frac{\text{Deflator}_{2025}}{\text{Deflator}_{t}}
\]
The same adjustment is applied to net principal. This provides a consistent U.S.-price adjustment for USD-denominated amounts; it is not a measure of Costa Rican inflation or purchasing power.

title: Methods
text:
Instrument Classification
Projects are classified as Investment Project Financing (IPF) or Development Policy Financing (DPL). Classification uses loan-type fields and project-name patterns, followed by a manual override file for reviewed exceptions.
The resulting categories are analytical classifications. They are not necessarily the formal instrument labels used at the time of approval. Automatic classifications, overrides, and override reasons are retained in the classification review output.

title: Methods
text:
Sector Analysis
Project sector allocations are drawn from API metadata, with project catalogue metadata used where necessary. Projects may have multiple sectors. Principal is allocated across reported sectors using their stated percentage shares:
\[
\text{Allocated principal} =
\text{Project principal}
\times
\frac{\text{Sector percentage}}{100}
\]
Reported percentages are not renormalized when they do not sum to 100%. Projects without usable percentage allocations do not contribute to sector-level dollar totals. Sector results therefore describe the subset of lending with usable allocation metadata, not the full portfolio.
Granular sector labels are consolidated into broader analytical groups for comparison across periods.

title: Methods
text:
Project Abstracts
Project abstracts are analyzed using six manually defined keyword groups: Infrastructure, Environment/Climate, Social Development, Governance/Fiscal, Competitiveness/Trade, and Disaster Risk.
The analysis measures keyword presence, not project outcomes or semantic themes. Period percentages use projects with available abstracts as the denominator. Periods without abstracts are treated as missing, not as zero.
Word frequencies are calculated after removing stop words and selected generic terms. These results are exploratory and sensitive to abstract availability and wording.

title: Methods
text:
IFC and MIGA
IFC disclosures are grouped by project number to avoid counting multiple disclosure documents as separate projects. Approved own-account amounts are extracted from the disclosure text. Actual approval dates are used where available; otherwise, projected Board dates provide indicative period assignments. Pipeline projects are excluded from the historical investment analysis.
MIGA disclosures are deduplicated by project. Repeated disclosures for the Papagayo project represent successive exposure records, not additive guarantees. The FY2003 record of $81 million is retained as the reported maximum exposure.

title: Methods
text:
Development Context
World Development Indicators are filtered to Costa Rica and the study period. Missing observations are retained; no interpolation is performed. The U.S. GDP deflator is applied only to IBRD financial amounts, not to the national development indicators.

title: Analysis
text:
The World Bank Group’s relationship with Costa Rica changed in scale, composition, and institutional form over 45 years. The evidence does not describe a straightforward progression from structural adjustment to investment to climate finance. Policy-based lending recurred across several decades; large investment operations appeared in concentrated bursts; and the available sector data provide only a partial view of the portfolio.
This analysis examines those patterns alongside Costa Rica’s economic trajectory. It distinguishes approved commitments from amounts ultimately retained or disbursed, and treats the IFC and MIGA portfolios separately from IBRD lending.

section: A. IBRD portfolio: scale and concentration
text:
A. IBRD portfolio: scale and concentration
IBRD lending was unevenly distributed across the study period. The 35 projects in the analytical sample account for approximately $4.6 billion in original principal, but the 2020–2025 period alone accounts for 12 projects and $2.7 billion, or 57.9% of the nominal total. The decade-level comparison therefore reflects a pronounced recent concentration, not a steady increase in lending.
The project count and commitment total tell different stories. The 2020s contain more operations than any earlier period, but their average size is also substantially larger. The top-ten portfolio reinforces this concentration: two $500 million development policy loans, approved in 2009 and 2023, and the $420 million health insurance operation approved in 2016 rank among the largest commitments. A relatively small number of large operations account for a substantial share of the portfolio.

title: Analysis
text:
B. Nominal and real commitments
Nominal totals exaggerate the apparent difference between recent and earlier lending because a dollar committed in 1980 did not have the same purchasing power as a dollar committed in 2025. Expressed in 2025 dollars using the US GDP deflator, the portfolio totals approximately $6.2 billion, compared with $4.6 billion in nominal terms.
The adjustment changes the scale of historical comparisons, but not the broad pattern. The 1980s’ eight operations total approximately $294 million nominally, equivalent to about $772 million in 2025 dollars. The $500 million 2009 development policy loan is equivalent to approximately $728 million. The 2020–2025 period remains the largest lending period in real terms, although its share of the inflation-adjusted portfolio is lower than its 57.9% nominal share.








Figure 2: Inflation adjustment increases the apparent scale of earlier lending, particularly in the 1980s; 2020–2025 remains the largest period in real terms.





These values adjust for changes in US prices, not Costa Rican purchasing power or the local cost of projects. They are a consistent basis for comparing the dollar value of commitments over time, not a measure of their domestic economic impact.

The 2009 operation was a large public-finance and competitiveness loan. The 2020s series focused on fiscal management and decarbonization. The 1990s also illustrate why approved commitments should not be read as completed lending. The decade includes a $100 million policy loan that was fully cancelled, while the investment portfolio includes the fully cancelled $41 million agriculture project. Instrument shares based on original commitments describe the approved portfolio; they do not describe financing ultimately delivered.

The small health-sector figure should not be read as evidence that health was a minor area of Bank engagement. Sector totals are therefore useful for describing the projects with usable allocation data, but not for ranking the Bank’s full portfolio by sector. The grouping of individual sectors into broader analytical categories is also a classification choice, not a World Bank classification.

title: Analysis
text:
E. Themes in project abstracts
Project abstracts provide a second, less quantitative view of changing engagement: the language used to describe what operations were intended to address. The available text suggests recurring attention to infrastructure, while governance and fiscal management become prominent in the later periods represented.








Figure 5: Governance and fiscal themes remain prominent, while environmental and climate language appears more frequently in recent abstracts. Uneven coverage limits comparisons across periods. Percentages describe keyword presence, not financing or outcomes.





Coverage is uneven. Abstracts are available for 19 of the 35 projects: two from the 1980s, none from the 1990s, seven from the 2000s, one from the 2010s, and nine from 2020–2025. The 2000s and 2020s provide the most useful comparison. In both, governance and fiscal themes appear frequently; environmental and climate language appears in four of seven 2000s abstracts and eight of nine recent abstracts.
The apparent increase in climate language is consistent with the greater prominence of climate and disaster-risk concerns in recent project descriptions. It is not, by itself, evidence of a corresponding increase in financing or results. The 1980s and 2010s samples are too small for meaningful comparisons, and the absence of 1990s abstracts prevents a continuous account.
The analysis identifies manually selected keyword groups in project abstracts (see Table 10). A match indicates that a theme appears in the text, not how much funding it received, how central it was to project design, or whether the project achieved its objectives. These results describe the available abstracts, not the Bank’s institutional priorities as a whole.

text:
F. Costa Rica’s development trajectory
IBRD lending took place alongside a substantial transformation in Costa Rica’s economy. GDP per capita, measured in constant 2015 US dollars, increased from approximately $6,224 in 1980 to $15,053 in 2024. Life expectancy rose from 73 to 81 years over the same period. Foreign direct investment became a more prominent feature—rising from roughly 1–3% of GDP in the 1980s to more than 8% in 2007, then stabilizing around 4–6% through the following decade—reflecting Costa Rica’s deeper integration into international investment and production networks. These long-run changes provide context for the lending relationship, but cannot be attributed to World Bank financing.

Its disclosed investments are heavily concentrated in financial services: approximately $678 million, or 77.6% of the investment total represented in the sector data. MIGA’s fiscal year runs from July through June. Earlier disclosures for the project should not be added together: they represent successive or cumulative records, not separate guarantees of equivalent value.

title: Analysis
text:
Conclusion
The evidence points to an uneven relationship shaped by changing instruments and a small number of large operations. Policy-based lending recurred across decades rather than giving way permanently to investment financing. The 2010s stand out for two large investment projects and no development policy loans; the 2020–2025 period stands out for both its scale and its balanced mix of policy and investment operations.
Costa Rica’s growing integration with international investment forms part of this wider context, while IFC and MIGA disclosures show the Group’s distinct private-sector and risk-guarantee roles. But the records do not support a single, unified measure of World Bank Group financing, nor do they establish that the Group caused the country’s economic and social changes.
The strongest conclusion is therefore about the changing character of the relationship, not a simple story of more lending or steadily shifting priorities. Its scale was concentrated, its instruments recurrent but differently applied, and its sectoral and thematic record incomplete.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica is a small country with a developmental track record that has never quite matched the standard template. It abolished its army in 1948 and spent the following decades building public education, health care, and social insurance institutions that became distinctive features of its model.
Those institutions were already substantial when this story begins in 1980. Costa Rica was not starting from scratch, and it was not simply waiting for an international lender to supply a development blueprint. Life expectancy was already rising; the state remained a major provider of essential services; and a domestic political tradition gave reform arguments a public, institutional setting rather than leaving them to a handful of technocrats.
Over the next 45 years, Costa Rica would face a debt crisis, liberalize and diversify its economy, build a world reputation for conservation, absorb major shocks, and eventually enter the World Bank’s high-income classification. The World Bank was present through much of that transformation, but its role changed with the country.
The central question is not only how much financing Costa Rica received. It is how the relationship between two changing development models evolved:

How did the World Bank Group’s financing relationship with Costa Rica change from 1980 to 2025 — in scale, instruments, and priorities — and what do those changes reveal about the practice of international development finance?

This is a descriptive story, not a study of causation. It follows the lending record and the institutional context around it, while leaving open a harder question: how much of the country’s trajectory reflected domestic choices, external pressures, private investment, and policy decisions for which no lending portfolio can take sole credit.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: Three institutions, three kinds of engagement
text:
Three institutions, three kinds of engagement
The phrase “the World Bank” usually means several different institutions within the World Bank Group.
The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) lends to creditworthy middle- and higher-income governments. Costa Rica’s 1980–2025 IBRD record is the core of this project: an approved-lending portfolio, not a record of every dollar actually delivered.
The International Finance Corporation (IFC) invests directly in private companies and financial institutions. Its own-account investments are different from IBRD sovereign loan principal.
The Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) provides political-risk guarantees to private investors. Its gross exposure is a potential liability, not a loan, a disbursement, or the value of an underlying project.
The figures for these institutions therefore cannot be added together. IBRD, IFC, and MIGA participated in Costa Rica’s development through different legal and financial instruments.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Forty-five years of IBRD lending
From 1980 through 2025, the IBRD record contains 35 projects with $4.6B in nominal original principal. In 2025 purchasing power, using the US GDP deflator, the same approved principal is roughly $6.2B.
Approved principal is the amount recorded when the IBRD Board approved an operation. It is not the same as funds signed, disbursed, or spent. That distinction becomes especially important in the story of SAL III, when a large approved operation never became an effective loan.








Figure 1: Annual IBRD lending to Costa Rica, 1980–2025. Bars show nominal original principal at Board approval and the same amounts adjusted to 2025 USD. Nominal and real values are separate representations of the same approved principal.





The timeline is the spine of this story. The country and the institution both changed around it.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: The 1980s: debt crisis and structural adjustment
text:
The 1980s: debt crisis and structural adjustment








Figure 2: IBRD lending in the 1980s. The 1983 Export Development Loan, 1985 SAL I, and 1988 SAL II are highlighted against the full 1980–2025 timeline.





Costa Rica entered the decade under severe pressure. A deteriorating terms of trade, rising international interest rates, domestic fiscal imbalances, commodity shocks, and regional instability culminated in a balance-of-payments and debt crisis. In August 1981, the government suspended debt-service payments to commercial creditors. Output fell sharply, unemployment rose, and inflation reached roughly 90 percent in 1982.
The response involved stabilization and structural reform. Costa Rica worked with the IMF, the World Bank, and bilateral donors to reduce inflation, liberalize trade, promote exports, and adjust the role of the state in the economy. The question was not simply how to restore foreign-exchange earnings. It was whether the country could change the way its economy worked without dismantling the public institutions that had been central to its model.
The World Bank’s contribution took several forms. The 1983 Export Development Loan supported export-sector and trade reforms. Structural Adjustment Loans I and II followed in 1985 and 1988. The same portfolio still contained identifiable investments: roads, water supply, petroleum support, and institutional assistance.
In the decade as a whole, eight IBRD projects approved roughly $294 million in nominal original principal. The three policy-based operations — the 1983 loan, SAL I, and SAL II — accounted for approximately 70 percent of that amount.
This period was an early negotiation over priorities rather than a clean transfer of a single economic model. Liberalization moved ahead, but Costa Rica’s public universities, health system, and social insurance institutions continued to operate. The result was neither the inward-looking economy that preceded the crisis nor a laissez-faire state. It was a more open hybrid, with market-oriented reforms sitting beside a persistent public role in social provision.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: The 1990s: a loan that never happened
text:
The 1990s: a loan that never happened








Figure 3: IBRD lending in the 1990s. SAL III was approved in 1993 but was cancelled in 1995 and never became effective or disbursed.





The 1993 Third Structural Adjustment Loan makes a concrete point about the limits of institutional plans. The IBRD approved $100 million, but Costa Rica’s incoming administration after the 1994 election did not meet the conditions needed for effectiveness. The loan was cancelled in March 1995 and disbursed no money.
That is a very different episode from a loan that was signed and later repaid. SAL III belongs in the history of Board-approved operations, but it never became delivered IBRD financing.
The failed effectiveness of SAL III also illustrates why “World Bank policy” and “Costa Rican policy” should not be treated as interchangeable. The Bank could propose terms and approve financing, but the next government had to act within domestic political processes to make the loan operational.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: The 1990s and 2000s: diversification and environmental finance
text:
The 1990s and 2000s: diversification and environmental finance








Figure 4: IBRD lending in the 2000s. Ecomarkets, the 2008 catastrophe contingent line, and the 2009 public finance and competitiveness DPL are highlighted.





Costa Rica’s economy was changing in a way no lending chart could capture by itself. Intel announced a major Costa Rican investment in 1996, and the country subsequently developed important export positions in medical devices and business services. Tourism grew as another source of foreign exchange and employment. The economic identity of the country was moving beyond its long reliance on traditional agriculture and becoming more integrated with global production and services.
Environmental policy followed a related but distinct domestic trajectory. Costa Rica established its national Payments for Environmental Services program, known as PSA, in 1997. The program compensated private landowners for maintaining forests and ecosystem services that markets otherwise undervalued.
In 2000, the World Bank approved the $32.6 million Ecomarkets project. It did not introduce forest conservation to Costa Rica. Instead, it supported an existing national initiative and helped strengthen the institutions and financing arrangements around it. This is a useful example of a shared priority: Costa Rica had developed the approach, and the Bank helped provide resources and institutional support.
Policy-based lending then returned. In 2008, the Bank approved the $65 million catastrophe deferred drawdown option, a contingent credit line for disasters. In 2009, a $500 million Development Policy Loan addressed public finance and competitiveness during the global financial crisis.
Policy-based finance never followed a simple forward-and-backward schedule. It returned under new circumstances, with a different immediate purpose.

MIGA and a private toll-road project
In FY2008, MIGA recorded gross guarantee exposure of $158.5 million for the Autopistas del Sol toll-road concession. MIGA’s guarantee protected private investors against specified political risks; it did not lend $158.5 million to Costa Rica or represent the concession’s total value.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: The 2010s: public institutions and private development
text:
The 2010s: public institutions and private development








Figure 5: IBRD lending in the 2010s. The two approvals supported higher education and universal health insurance.





The 2010s provide a reminder that a sparse decade in project count need not be a small decade in financing. IBRD approved just two projects, with combined original principal of $620 million.
The 2012 Higher Education Improvement Project provided $200 million to strengthen Costa Rica’s public university system. The 2016 operation, Strengthening Universal Health Insurance, provided $420 million to the Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social, the institution that administers public health insurance.
At $420 million, the health operation was the largest Investment Project Financing operation in the 1980–2025 IBRD portfolio. The small number of projects conceals the scale of support directed to major public institutions.
IFC engaged through a different channel. Rather than financing government programs, it invested in private companies. The Reventazón hydropower project was a prominent 2012 example: a $100 million IFC own-account investment in a major private-sector energy asset. That amount is not IBRD principal and should not be combined with it.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: The 2020s: fiscal reform, climate, and pandemic
text:
The 2020s: fiscal reform, climate, and pandemic








Figure 6: IBRD lending in the 2020s. The 2020, 2021, and 2023 Fiscal and Decarbonization Management DPLs are highlighted against the full timeline.





The 2020–2025 period is the portfolio’s high-concentration period. It includes 12 projects and $2.66 billion in nominal original principal — 57.9 percent of all 1980–2025 approved principal.
Several domestic developments explain why fiscal management became central. Costa Rica faced a 2017 fiscal and liquidity crisis, then adopted contested tax reform in 2018. In 2019, the country launched the National Decarbonization Plan, setting an ambition to reach net-zero emissions by 2050. The COVID-19 pandemic then disrupted economic activity and public finances in 2020.
The IBRD’s response included a series of Fiscal and Decarbonization Management Development Policy Loans:

$300 million in 2020
$300 million in 2021
$500 million in 2023

A second disaster-risk DPL with a contingent drawdown option was approved in 2023 at $160 million. The 2025 portfolio continued the mix with fiscal and green-growth policy support, a sustainable agriculture investment, education, territorial development, and social risk management.
These DPLs provided budget support tied to policy commitments. They were not direct financing for green infrastructure. The 2020–2023 sequence matters: Costa Rica articulated its decarbonization ambition in 2019, before the Bank’s climate-linked DPL series began.
The interpretation is therefore not that the Bank introduced climate policy to Costa Rica. It was incorporating a national ambition into a broader financing relationship centered on fiscal sustainability, public policy, and recovery from a pandemic.
The portfolio remained mixed even at the height of policy lending. Education, agriculture, disaster resilience, territorial development, fisheries, tax administration, and social protection all continued to receive investment financing.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica’s development trajectory








Figure 7: Costa Rica’s development trajectory, 1980–2025. Real income and life expectancy improved substantially, while the Gini index reveals a less complete story of social success.





The lending timeline unfolded alongside substantial social and economic change. In real 2015 US dollars, GDP per capita rose from approximately $6,200 in 1980 to $15,100 in 2024. Life expectancy increased from approximately 73 years to 81 years.
Inequality complicates the success story. The Gini index peaked at roughly 51.8 in 2002 in this series, then declined to 45.8 in 2024. A 2025 World Bank API estimate is around 45.5, but it is preliminary rather than a confirmed survey observation.
These patterns are context, not evidence that World Bank lending caused income growth, health gains, or inequality trends. Costa Rica’s trajectory reflected public institutions, demographic change, trade, foreign investment, social policy, and the country’s own political decisions. The lending record can show an evolving partnership, but it cannot isolate one institution’s contribution to the national outcome.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: IBRD lending by instrument: the visual recap
text:
IBRD lending by instrument: the visual recap








Figure 8: IBRD lending by instrument type. Development Policy Loans provide budget support tied to policy commitments; Investment Project Financing supports identifiable programs and capital projects. Earlier policy-based operations are grouped with DPLs for a historical comparison.





The instrument mix closes the chronology. Development Policy Loans provide budget support in return for policy commitments. Investment Project Financing supports identifiable programs and capital projects. The historical category includes earlier structural adjustment and policy-based operations that served a similar function before the modern instrument labels became standardized.
The instruments did not replace one another in a straight line. Policy-based lending was dominant in the 1980s, nearly absent in the 2010s, and prominent again in the 2020s. Investment Project Financing accompanied adjustment, continued through the diversification period, and financed major public institutions in the 2010s.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Conclusion: a changing relationship
Costa Rica’s development story is not reducible to the institutions that financed it. Its social model predated this study. Its economic identity changed through domestic decisions and global forces. Its forest and climate ambitions emerged through public policy that other institutions could support but did not originate.
The World Bank changed too. It moved from adjustment-era policy lending toward social investment, environmental finance, public-sector support, and climate-linked fiscal operations. Those changes were real, but they did not create a simple sequence in which the Bank replaced one philosophy with the next. Different instruments coexisted and returned under different circumstances.
Approval also remained distinct from delivery. The 1993 SAL III approval was cancelled. The vaccine operation in 2022 was terminated before the loan agreement. The 2009 DPL was different again: a large operation approved for public finance and competitiveness in the midst of a global crisis.
The relationship was never simply a lender directing a borrower. It was an evolving negotiation among Costa Rica’s development choices, the priorities of a domestic political system, and an international institution’s changing ideas about development finance.
In 1980, Costa Rica was responding to a debt crisis. By 2025, it had become a high-income economy. Its next set of development questions is not whether it can reproduce the social model of the earlier era under a new income classification, but how it can sustain and broaden that model amid fiscal pressure, inequality, climate risk, and a changing private economy.
For the World Bank, the question is equally important: what does development finance look like when the borrower is no longer conventionally poor?

Financial measures
IBRD loan records distinguish approved commitments from subsequent financial activity.

Definition




Original principal
Board-approved loan amount, nominal USD

Original principal is assigned to the loan’s Board Approval Year. Disbursements and repayments are cumulative snapshot values, not annual flows.
IBRD guarantees are excluded from the loan analysis. No guarantees were identified in the Costa Rica loan records.

title: Data
text:
Source-specific qualifications
Project dates. The Projects & Operations catalogue supplies canonical project approval dates. These were checked against API V3 date-recovery records. The IBRD Statement’s Board Approval Date is used separately to assign approval years to loan-level financial records.
IBRD coverage. The API V2 extract does not contain every project appearing in the catalogue or loan statement. The $420 million Health Insurance project (P148435), approved in 2016, is present in the loan statement and project catalogue but absent from the V2 extract. The loan statement is authoritative for the financial analysis.
IFC investments. Amounts represent IFC own-account investment, not total project financing or syndicated funding. Most investment records have projected Board dates; dates and period assignments should therefore be treated as indicative. The pending Insulet project is excluded from the historical study period.
MIGA guarantees. Fiscal-year labels are retained as published. Gross exposure represents maximum guarantee liability. Repeated disclosures for the Papagayo tourism project are not additive; the FY2003 record of $81 million is retained.
Inflation adjustment. The U.S. GDP deflator adjusts USD commitments for changes in U.S. prices. It does not measure Costa Rican purchasing power or local inflation. The 2025 deflator observation may be revised.

title: Data
text:
Scope and exclusions
The primary financial analysis covers IBRD sovereign lending approved from 1980 through 2025. IFC investments and MIGA guarantees are presented separately because their financial measures represent different forms of development finance.
The study does not cover bilateral assistance, IMF or IDB financing, domestic borrowing, or private investment beyond the disclosed IFC and MIGA records.
